read_scope.notes: Read all 22 PDF pages in full, including the references and Appendices A-G. Rendered and visually inspected every page, including Figures 1-5 and Tables 1-10. Consulted the frozen paper.tex and specificity_results.tex for exact wording and source locations. Treated appendix derivations and supporting cohorts as optional depth when assessing main-text accessibility. The abstract has 149 whitespace-delimited words in the supplied TeX. Independently computed the supplied PDF SHA256. No other reviews, earlier manuscripts, repository results, or external sources were consulted.

score_reasons.expression: Excellent, precise English with manageable sentences and unusually clear distinctions between a measured response, reference agreement, and perceptual artistic fidelity. Section 4.1 explains contrasts before introducing notation, and the results repeatedly translate numerical differences into their meaning. The remaining language issues are localized: feature rescaling can momentarily be confused with coordinate standardization, and the source-sensitivity passage carries several numerical qualifications in quick succession.
score_reasons.structure: The question, controlled prompt design, feature representation, score intuition, inference, and findings form a coherent progression. Section 5.1 establishes the primary result; Sections 5.3-5.5 then explain artist coverage, calibration, scene dependence, and source sensitivity. The changed Sunburst comparison is flagged at its first presentation and revisited explicitly. Appendix placement keeps derivations, historical cohorts, and extensive diagnostics from becoming prerequisites for the main argument. Only minor tightening of the final results subsection would improve emphasis.
score_reasons.new_reader_understanding: The abstract stands alone within its length limit, and the main text identifies the six conditions, finite digital reference target, development scaling, and fixed-scene scope without requiring repository access. The Monet-Sisley lightness example and the idealized D values of 1, 0, and 1 make the central comparison understandable. Tables explain benchmark values and the image panels show what is being compared. Local refinements remain in specifying exactly what calibration rescales and in making the negative pair-error estimate self-explanatory in Figure 3.
score_reasons.engagement: The opening Monet-versus-Sisley example poses a consequential and concrete evaluation problem. Figure 1 rewards direct inspection of prompt conditions, Figure 2 supplies useful magnified details, and Figure 3 makes uneven artist coverage easy to locate. The GPT Image 2 calibration reversal and Nano Banana 2 scene-averaging reversal give the results a discernible narrative. Momentum softens in Section 5.5 as multiple sensitivity settings, crop counts, error estimates, and inferential qualifications accumulate before the final takeaway; this is a limited weakness in an otherwise engaging scientific account.

strengths: Section 4.1 uses the measured Monet-Sisley lightness gap (.325 reference units versus .254 for GPT Image 2) to explain centering, then uses three idealized generators to distinguish aligned response from total error.

The main results preserve the central asymmetry: every aligned-response interval is positive, but no model is established to beat the no-distinction benchmark. The prose does not turn unresolved superiority into evidence of equivalence.

Figure 1 displays all six conditions for all six generators under one disclosed selection rule; its caption distinguishes the historical reproductions from generator inputs and matched compositions. The rendered gallery makes the experiment tangible.

Figure 2 uses shared overview axes and magnified Monet/Sisley/Pissarro details, while Figure 3 supplies direct numerical pair summaries. Their captions explain both their reading conventions and the limits of the projections or scores.

Table 3 and its surrounding text explain why changing response strength or averaging over scenes can reverse model orderings, while explicitly separating these measured-feature operations from improved images.
The original and retrospectively corrected comparisons remain visibly separate, and Table 4 shows the changed interval conclusions rather than presenting only the unchanged lowest point estimate.

findings.location: Abstract, p. 1 (paper.tex line 37); Section 4.4, p. 6 (paper.tex lines 307-313); Table 3 caption, p. 9
findings.issue: The phrases feature rescaling, rescales measured features, and rescales feature vectors are broader than the operation actually performed: one multiplier is applied to each model's centered generated painter contrasts while the reference contrasts remain fixed. The paper also uses scaling for development-panel coordinate standardization and its source-corrected refit.
findings.reader_effect: A new reader can briefly interpret the ordering reversal as a change of feature units or metric instead of a fitted change in the strength of the generated contrasts. Section 5.4 and Appendix B.1 eventually resolve this, so the ambiguity is localized.
findings.suggested_change: Use rescaling of generated contrasts in the abstract and centered generated contrasts in the Table 3 caption. In Section 4.4, replace the broad calibration sentence with: Calibration multiplies only the centered generated contrasts; reference contrasts and coordinate units stay fixed. Retain the existing statement that images are unchanged. These substitutions can stay within the 155-word abstract and 22-page limits.

findings.issue: The source-sensitivity takeaway is preceded by a list of window, target, weighting, and texture checks, and then accompanied by crop counts, two corrected FLUX values, a corrected calibrated value, and three changed model comparisons. The distinction between a stable lowest point estimate and changing interval conclusions is clear but has to compete with this numerical inventory.
findings.reader_effect: The final results subsection slows the narrative just as it reaches its most consequential qualification: source handling changes which model differences are resolved.
findings.suggested_change: Condense the opening sensitivity list into one sentence with an appendix pointer. Move the texture-only values 1.580/1.604 and the intermediate original-scaling crop value .832 into the relevant appendix passage; keep the original-to-refitted comparison .801 to .872 and Table 4 in the main text. This preserves the evidence while giving the changed interval conclusions more emphasis without increasing total length.

findings.issue: The caption explains zero, one, and negative values for pair aligned response, but explains only one for pair error even though the error panel contains a negative estimate (-.05 for Nano Banana 2, Sisley-Pissarro).
findings.reader_effect: A reader inspecting the heatmap has to recall the explanation on p. 5 to distinguish a small negative corrected estimate from a claim of better-than-perfect agreement.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the pair-error sentence with a compact explanation that expected error is zero for exact agreement and one for no distinction, and that negative estimates can arise from the repeat-noise correction. This can replace existing caption wording rather than add a new paragraph.

summary: An excellent and largely self-contained account of a bounded digital-reference comparison. The central distinction between response detection and agreement is readily understood, the primary and retrospective results are clearly separated, and the figures support the argument. Remaining improvements are localized wording, emphasis, and caption refinements; no substantive claim-fidelity problem was identified within the rubric's editorial scope.
